'''Nora Owen''' ({{nee|'''O'Mahony'''}}; born 1 June 1945) is an Irish former [[Fine Gael]] politician who served as [[Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration|Minister for Justice]] from 1994 to 1997 and [[Leader of Fine Gael#Deputy leaders|Deputy leader of Fine Gael]] from 1993 to 2001. She served as a [[Teachta Dála]] (TD) for the [[Dublin North (Dáil constituency)|Dublin North]] constituency from 1981 to 1987 and 1989 to 2002.<ref name=oireachtas_db>{{cite web|url=https://www.oireachtas.ie/en/members/member/Nora-Owen.D.1981-06-30/|title=Nora Owen|work=Oireachtas Members Database|date=23 April 2002|access-date=24 January 2010|archive-date=26 October 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201026152538/https://www.oireachtas.ie/en/members/member/Nora-Owen.D.1981-06-30/|url-status=live}}</ref>

She was a presenter of [[TV3 (Ireland)|TV3]]'s topical programme ''Midweek''.

==Early life==
Owen was born in [[Dublin]] in 1945. She is a sister of [[Mary Banotti]] and a grandniece of the Irish revolutionary leader [[Michael Collins (Irish leader)|Michael Collins]]. She was educated at Dominican Convent, [[County Wicklow]] and [[University College Dublin]] (UCD) where she qualified as an industrial chemist.

==Political career==
Owen was first elected to [[Dublin County Council]] in 1979 for the [[Malahide]] local electoral area. She was later elected as a [[Fine Gael]] TD for the first time in 1981, serving until the 1987 election when she lost her seat. That year she became a member of the executive of [[Trócaire]]. She returned to [[Dáil Éireann]] following the [[1989 Irish general election|1989 general election]]. In 1993, she became Deputy leader of Fine Gael. The following year she became [[Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration|Minister for Justice]], remaining in that post until 1997. She undertook a significant programme of criminal law reform.<ref name=mcnamara>McNamara, Maedhbh. A woman's place is in the Cabinet: women ministers in Irish governments 1919-2019. Drogheda, Sea Dog Books,2020.ISBN 978-1-913275-06-8</ref> Among the major changes she implemented was the referendum on bail in 1996, leading to the Bail Act, of 1997, which allows a court to refuse bail to those charged with a serious offence where it is considered necessary to prevent them committing a serious offence.<ref name=mcnamara/> Journalist [[Veronica Guerin]] was murdered in 1996 and in its aftermath, Owen introduced the highly successful [[Criminal Assets Bureau]] to crack down on [[organised crime]]. In 2002, she became the first high-profile [[Fine Gael]] TD to lose her seat in [[Dublin North (Dáil constituency)|Dublin North]] in the party's disastrous [[2002 Irish general election|general election]] result.<ref name=elecs_irl>{{cite web|url=http://electionsireland.org/candidate.cfm?ID=3305|title=Nora Owen|work=ElectionsIreland.org|access-date=24 January 2010|archive-date=21 February 2011|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110221192141/http://electionsireland.org/candidate.cfm?id=3305|url-status=live}}</ref>

==Post-political life==
Owen is the patron of the [[Collins 22 Society]], which works to keep the memory and legacy of Michael Collins in living memory. She occasionally works as an election pundit. In August 2011, it was announced she was to present the Irish version of ''[[Mastermind (Irish game show)|Mastermind]]'' on [[TV3 (Ireland)|TV3]].<ref>{{cite news|url=http://www.irishtimes.com/newspaper/ireland/2011/0819/1224302708476.html|title=TV3 mixes some highbrow with reality for autumn|newspaper=[[The Irish Times]]|date=19 August 2011|access-date=26 August 2011|archive-date=20 August 2011|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110820114059/http://www.irishtimes.com/newspaper/ireland/2011/0819/1224302708476.html|url-status=live}}</ref>
